---
title: "Getting started"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
requireNamespace("xts", quietly = TRUE)
```

fcutils is a set of functions for the time series work behind UHERO's
forecasts. A forecast at UHERO starts from the history of many
series, such as payroll jobs or visitor arrivals. Each series is then
extended to a date some years ahead, using assumptions about growth or
levels. The results are summarised as annual averages, growth rates,
tables and plots. fcutils covers each of those steps: getting data,
converting between formats and frequencies, extending series into the
forecast period, and showing the results.

This article covers what every script needs first: the bank options, the
data formats the functions accept, series names and how to write dates.
[Building a forecast](forecasting.html) and
[Growth rates, tables and plots](growth-and-reporting.html) follow on from
it.

Install the package from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("UHERO/fcutils")
```

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(fcutils)
```

## The bank

A forecast holds many series, and they need to share the same dates so
that they can be added, divided and compared. fcutils calls that common
date range the *bank*: it runs from the start of the history to the end of
the forecast period. `make_xts()`, `addf()`, `extend()` and `span()`
without dates return series that cover the whole bank, and they
read its first and last date from two options. Set them once at the top of
a script, before calling any of these functions:

```{r}
options(
  fcutils.bnk_start = as.Date("1990-01-01"),
  fcutils.bnk_end = as.Date("2035-12-31")
)
```

Without the options, those functions stop with an error saying so.
`make_xts()` builds an empty or constant series on the bank, or a series
from a vector of values:

```{r}
make_xts(per = "quarter", val = 0) |> head(3)
make_xts(2024.1, per = "quarter", val = c(1.5, 1.7, 1.6))
```

## Data formats

R holds time series in several ways, and fcutils takes most of them. A
*wide* data frame has a `time` column and one column per series. A *long*
data frame stacks the series in three columns, `id` (the series name),
`time` and `value`. An xts object is a matrix of values with dates
attached to the rows, from the
[xts](https://joshuaulrich.github.io/xts/) package; it is convenient for
arithmetic and for subsetting by date. The functions accept all of these,
along with anything else that the
[tsbox](https://docs.ropensci.org/tsbox/) package reads, such as base R's
ts. They return the result in the format of the input.

The package ships three wide tibbles of Hawaii data from UDAMAN, UHERO's
data system: `quarterly_data_example` (payroll jobs by industry,
1998–2025, in thousands), `monthly_data_example` (visitor arrivals and
related series, in thousands) and `daily_data_example` (visitor arrivals
by day, 2020–2022).

```{r}
q <- quarterly_data_example[, c("time", "E_NF_HI", "ECT_HI")]
tail(q, 3)
```

`agg()` averages quarters to years. Given a wide tibble it returns a wide
tibble, and given xts it returns xts:

```{r}
agg(q) |> tail(3)
agg(conv_xts(q)) |> tail(3)
```

`conv_long()`, `conv_wide()`, `conv_xts()` and `conv_tslist()` convert
between formats. Unlike `tsbox::ts_long()`, `conv_long()` takes wide data
frames and gives a single series an `id` column:

```{r}
conv_long(q) |> head(3)
conv_long(conv_xts(q)$E_NF_HI) |> head(3)
```

## Series names

The examples use UHERO's series names. A name is a mnemonic for the
concept, an `@`, the geography and a frequency: `E_NF@HI.Q` is nonfarm
payroll jobs (`E_NF`) in Hawaii (`HI`), quarterly (`Q`). When fcutils
downloads a series it drops the frequency and replaces `@` with `_`, so
the column is called `E_NF_HI`. The series used below are:

| Name | Series |
|---|---|
| `E_NF_HI` | nonfarm payroll jobs, all industries |
| `ECT_HI` | construction jobs |
| `EAF_HI` | accommodation and food services jobs |
| `EGV_HI` | government jobs |
| `VISNS_HI` | visitor arrivals, not seasonally adjusted (`NS`) |

## Dates

Wherever a function takes a date, `to_ymd()` reads it. A year, a quarter
or a day can be a number or a string; as a number, a quarter is either a
decimal (`2024.3`) or six digits (`202403`). A month must be a string,
because R stores `2024.10` and `2024.1` as the same number.

```{r}
to_ymd(c("2024", "2024Q3", "2024M10", "2024-10-15"))
to_ymd(c(2024, 2024.3, 202403, 20241015))
```

`p()` turns two dates into the range string that xts uses for subsetting.
A year or a quarter given as the end is included in full:

```{r}
x <- conv_xts(q)$E_NF_HI
x[p(2024.2, 2024)]
```

`span()` cuts any format to a range. `find_start()` and `find_end()` give
the first and last date with a value:

```{r}
span(q, 2024) |> head(3)
find_end(q)
```

With `extend = TRUE`, `span()` also pads a series with NA out to the end
of the range:

```{r}
span(x, 2024.4, 2025.4, extend = TRUE)
```

Without any dates, `span()` fits a series to the bank: it cuts the series
at the bank's start and end and pads it with NA to both. Use it to put a
series made some other way, such as an annual average from `agg()`, on the
same dates as the rest of the bank:

```{r}
span(x) |> tsbox::ts_summary()
```

## Getting data

These functions need network access and keys, so this page does not run
them.

`get_series()` downloads series from UDAMAN, UHERO's data system, by name.
`get_series_exp()` downloads every series in a UDAMAN export. Both need the
UDAMAN token, stored once with `set_udaman_token()` (or as `udaman_token` in
`.Renviron`), and the UHERO VPN unless `public = TRUE`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
get_series(c("VISNS@HI.M", "E_NF@HI.Q"))
get_series_exp(74, format = "xts")
```

`get_series_src()` downloads from FRED, Statistics Canada, the Bank of
Canada, Japan's e-Stat and the EIA. FRED, e-Stat and the EIA need a key,
stored with `set_api_key()` or in `.Renviron` (`FRED_API_KEY`,
`ESTAT_API_KEY`, `EIA_API_KEY`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
get_series_src("UNRATE", "fred")
get_series_src(c("PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL"), "fred", format = "xts")
```

forecast period.
